section_1.title: Prerequisite Warm-up: The Probability Space
section_1.content: Visualizing Conditional Probability as 'shrinking the universe.' Introduce the concept of P(A|B) using a Venn diagram where the sample space narrows from the total area to only the area covered by event B.
section_1.example: A square representing 100 students; highlight the circle of 'Math majors' (B) and the sub-circle of 'Data Science students' (A) within B.

section_2.title: Defining Independence: Does B change A?
section_2.content: Mathematically, A and B are independent if P(A|B) = P(A). Visually, this means knowing B happened provides zero 'new' information about A. We animate this by showing the slice of A remaining identical in size regardless of whether we filter by B or not.
section_2.example: Flipping a coin (Event A) and rolling a die (Event B). The outcome of the die roll doesn't physically squeeze or expand the probability space of the coin flip.

section_3.title: Bayes' Theorem: The Logic of Reverse Prediction
section_3.content: Introducing the theorem: P(A|B) = [P(B|A) * P(A)] / P(B). Explain this as a 'Correction Formula'—updating our prior belief P(A) based on new evidence B. Use an animated balance scale where evidence tips the probability of a hypothesis.
section_3.example: A 'Robot Doctor' trying to diagnose a patient. Event A: Patient has a flu. Event B: Patient has a cough. We know P(Cough|Flu), but we need the inverse: P(Flu|Cough).

section_4.title: Synthesis & Application: The Diagnostic Power
section_4.content: Combining both concepts. Show how independence simplifies Bayesian calculations. If events are independent, the theorem collapses, but if they are dependent (common in real life), the 'Likelihood Ratio' effectively updates our knowledge.
section_4.example: A smart home sensor detecting a fire. We weigh the prior probability of fire (very low) against the evidence of smoke (high accuracy), showing how Bayes' prevents 'False Alarm' panic by keeping the prior in check.
